items.summary: Table Of Contents Table of Contents How AI Penetration Testing Frameworks Work AI Penetration Testing Frameworks in Real-World Attacks What Flashpoint Is Seeing on Underground Forums How AI Is Changing the Cyberattack Lifecycle How Organizations Can Defend Against AI-Assisted Attacks What’s Next for AI Penetration Testing Frameworks? More subscribe to our newsletter On November 13, 2026, the FBI warned that threat actors are misusing autonomous AI penetration testing frameworks, including ARTEX, to conduct cyber intrusions. Security researchers have also documented the use of Cairn, HexStrike AI, and AntiFox in campaigns involving mass exploitation, credential theft, and unauthorized access to enterprise environments. Flashpoint’s research reveals growing interest in these tools across underground forums, where cybercriminals are seeking training, unrestricted AI models, and operational partners. While the technology is evolving, reported attacks have largely exploited familiar weaknesses: unpatched vulnerabilities, weak credentials, and exposed cloud secrets. AI is making these attacks faster and easier to execute at scale. How AI Penetration Testing Frameworks Work AI penetration testing frameworks connect large language models (LLMs) to security tools and testing environments, allowing them to automate portions of the penetration testing process. Instead of relying on a human operator to select each command, interpret results, and determine the next step, these frameworks use an automated loop to execute tools, analyze their output, and decide what to do next. Their capabilities range from reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning to exploitation and post-exploitation activity. Originally developed for authorized security testing, these tools have expanded rapidly. GitGuardian identified approximately 45 open source frameworks, many built on existing projects or sharing similar designs. Several have appeared in reported malicious activity: Framework Reported malicious use ARTEX Automated reconnaissance and exploitation in campaigns attributed to China-nexus actors Cairn Intrusions targeting semiconductor and defense organizations HexStrike AI Underground discussions linking the tool to exploitation of Citrix NetScaler vulnerabilities AntiFox Web shell deployment and theft of AWS secrets Strix Used alongside Cairn in reported exploitation activity PentAGI and CyberStrikeAI Identified in activity targeting financial organizations Because these frameworks are publicly available, their presence in an intrusion does not establish attribution. Legitimate security researchers, cybercriminals, and state-linked actors may use the same tools. AI Penetration Testing Frameworks in Real-World Attacks Security researchers have documented several campaigns involving AI penetration testing frameworks. In September 2025, Check Point reported underground discussions claiming HexStrike AI was being used to exploit newly disclosed Citrix NetScaler vulnerabilities. Some actors subsequently advertised compromised appliances for sale. More recently, CrowdStrike linked ARTEX to a China-nexus campaign targeting more than 200 organizations. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 separately reported that China-nexus actors conducted 25 operations against at least 19 organizations between August and September 2026, gaining access to data at 10. Targets included organizations in the semiconductor and defense sectors. Arctic Wolf also identified AntiFox instances hosted on Alibaba Cloud that were used to deploy web shells and steal AWS secrets. Across these cases, frameworks supported activities including automated reconnaissance, exploitation of known vulnerabilities, and credential theft. Most reported intrusions relied on existing security weaknesses rather than previously unknown exploits. What Flashpoint Is Seeing on Underground Forums Flashpoint’s monitoring of underground communities shows cybercriminals actively exploring how to incorporate AI penetration testing tools into their operations. On Russian-language forums, discussions center on training, model access, and collaboration. In October 2026, a user on Exploit requested tutoring in CyberStrike, HexStrike, and PentAGI. Another user on Rehub sought training with the same tools to gain initial access to networks, offering to work for free in exchange for experience. Other participants discussed obtaining uncensored versions of GLM and DeepSeek, while one forum member claimed to have built an AI penetration testing bot and offered free scans. Flashpoint also observed advertisements for AI model relay services in a Chinese-language Telegram community associated with ARTEX. Despite this interest, analysts did not observe sales of cracked or hosted frameworks on the monitored forums and marketplaces. For now, demand appears concentrated on learning to use the technology rather than purchasing ready-made attack services. A $10,000 Contest Highlights Criminal Interest in AI-Assisted Attacks In August 2026, a member of the Russian-language Exploit forum announced a hacking article contest offering a US$10,000 prize paid in bitcoin. AI-assisted attacks were among the suggested topics. Flashpoint analysts identified at least seven submissions, two focused on using AI to compromise networks. One article, AI Pentest from A to Z , described using AI to identify vulnerable systems across industries, automate exploitation of known flaws, and audit software for vulnerabilities. It also discussed monetizing access through credential theft and other malicious activities. Another submission, AI Hacking Without Refusals: My OpenCode, DeepSeek, and Claude Setup , described attempts to bypass model safety restrictions and use leaked API keys to support attacks. These accounts reflect the authors’ claims, not independently verified attack outcomes. The contest also generated a dispute over an alleged $3,500 arrangement to deploy malicious lures on compromised websites. Flashpoint could not verify either party’s account. The submissions provide a view into how established cybercriminal communities are experimenting with AI-assisted intrusion techniques and exploring ways to monetize them. How AI Is Changing the Cyberattack Lifecycle AI penetration testing frameworks largely rely on the same tools and techniques used in conventional penetration testing. Frameworks such as ARTEX automate portions of the decision-making process through agentic loops, allowing them to execute tasks, interpret results, and determine subsequent actions with less human intervention. Based on reported intrusions and underground discussions, Flashpoint identified several ways threat actors are integrating AI into existing attack workflows. Attack stage AI-assisted activity Model access Obtaining subscriptions, leaked API keys, or unrestricted models Guardrail evasion Attempting to bypass model safety restrictions Reconnaissance Identifying targets, exposed infrastructure, and vulnerable software Exploitation Automating attacks against known vulnerabilities Targeted testing Using specialized frameworks against individual high-value targets Vulnerability discovery Auditing source code for previously unknown weaknesses Monetization Supporting credential theft, access sales, and other criminal activity Not every actor uses every stage, and some techniques are drawn from unverified underground claims. The underlying attack methods have not fundamentally changed. What AI adds is speed and efficiency. Tasks that previously required an operator to manually interpret results and select the next action can now run in automated sequences, allowing attackers to move through established attack workflows faster and test more targets simultaneously. How Organizations Can Defend Against AI-Assisted Attacks Flashpoint analysts assess that AI penetration testing frameworks currently pose the greatest risk by accelerating exploitation of known weaknesses. Organizations should focus on the vulnerabilities and misconfigurations these tools are already being used to exploit: Prioritize internet-facing vulnerabilities. Accelerate remediation when public exploit code is available or exploitation has been observed. Strengthen authentication. Enforce MFA across administrative interfaces, partner portals, and legacy applications. Eliminate default credentials. Protect API keys and cloud secrets. Remove exposed credentials from code and configuration files, rotate unused keys, and restrict AI provider credentials. Monitor automated activity. Investigate unusual request volumes, repeated authentication failures, and unexpected cloud identity activity. Identify exposed security tools. Review internet-facing systems for unauthorized framework consoles and unrecognized installations. Conduct authorized AI-assisted testing. Use these frameworks to identify weaknesses in your own environment before attackers exploit them. What’s Next for AI Penetration Testing Frameworks? Flashpoint analysts assess with moderate confidence that malicious use of these frameworks will increase in 2027. The tools are widely accessible, inexpensive to operate, and easily copied, making individual repository takedowns unlikely to stop their use. One development to watch is the emergence of hosted, pay-per-use attack services. Such offerings could make autonomous intrusion capabilities accessible to criminals without requiring them to configure the tools themselves. For defenders, the priority remains reducing exposure to known vulnerabilities, compromised credentials, and misconfigured systems before automated tools can exploit them. items.title: Government Requests for User Data in 2026: Who Asks, Who Hands It Over
items.summary: Governments asked Google, Apple, Meta and Microsoft for user data 1,509,759 times in 2025. In four cases out of five, they got some. That is 21% more than in 2024 and six times the 2015 figure. The total has grown every single year of the past ten. This page puts the transparency reports of 18 companies side by side: who asks, how often the answer is yes, what each service can hand over, and what changed in the law in 2026. The core numbers are for calendar 2025, the last full year that every large company has reported. Where a company has already published the first half of 2026, we show that too. Key findings 1,509,759 requests for user data reached Google, Apple, Meta and Microsoft in 2025: 21% more than in 2024 and 6.2 times the 2015 figure. 80% of them ended with some data handed over. Microsoft said no most often and produced data in 65% of cases. India sent 31% of all requests (465,050), 50% more than a year earlier. Germany asks the most per person: 186 requests per 100,000 people. 128,922 were emergency requests, sent without a court order: one in twelve, three quarters of them to Meta. Secret US FISA orders for content covered at least 388,500 Google accounts in 2025, more than one and a half times the 241,752 accounts named in all ordinary US requests to Google. AI chatbots are the fastest-growing target: OpenAI received 794 requests in the first half of 2026, against 455 in all of 2025.

items.title: AI’s Third Product-Market Fit Will Be Won in the SOC
items.summary: AI’s future in cybersecurity is an integrated SOC – Aimei Wei , Founder, CTO at Stellar Cyber San Jose, Calif. – Nov. 23, 2026 Tomasz Tunguz recently argued that cybersecurity may become AI’s third major product-market fit, after coding and customer support. He’s not wrong, but his data points to something even more important for security teams: AI is arriving across parts of security operations that have traditionally been treated as separate disciplines. Tunguz’s analysis shows security spending across the SOC , SIEM and log ingestion, penetration testing, threat intelligence, and vulnerability management, alongside the AI token intensity of each. His point is about the growing role of AI across all five, but my takeaway is architectural, and goes a bit further. These functions increasingly need to work together. AI Needs Evidence, Not More Data Security teams already have enormous amounts of telemetry. From endpoints, networks, identities, firewalls, SaaS applications, cloud infrastructure, vulnerability scanners, and threat intelligence, the problem is certainly not just more data. The problem is turning that data into evidence that an analyst, or an AI system, can use to make a decision. Consider a suspicious identity. To understand what actually happened, an investigation may need to connect an unusual login with workload access, endpoint activity, network behavior, vulnerabilities, and threat intelligence. If those signals remain trapped in different tools and data models, AI inherits the same problem analysts have struggled with for years: it has to reconstruct the attack one system at a time. That is why the AI SOC is fundamentally an architecture problem. Different Problems Require Different AI Security operations cannot depend on one form of AI. Machine learning can identify unusual behavior across large datasets. Graph analytics can connect users, assets, alerts, and activity. Large language models can interpret evidence and help analysts understand it. Agentic AI can investigate observables, test hypotheses, and recommend or execute approved actions. At Stellar Cyber, we call this Multi-Layer AI . What matters, however, is not how many AI techniques you can name. What matters is whether they work from the same evidence and within the same security workflow. Detection cannot remain separate from investigation, and investigation cannot remain separate from response. The evidence that produced a decision must follow that decision through the process. This is the architectural premise behind the Integrated Security Operations Center, or ISOC . AI Changes the SOC Operating Model Tunguz makes another important observation: attackers can use AI to parallelize their efforts. Defenders need to do the same. That doesn’t just mean putting another AI agent inside every security product. It means enabling AI to work across identity, endpoint, network, cloud, vulnerabilities, and threat intelligence as parts of the same investigation. AI then stops being another feature in the security stack and starts changing how the SOC itself operates. This distinction will become more important as AI use grows. The future SOC should not be measured by how many models it runs, agents it deploys, or tokens it consumes. It should be measured by whether it identifies the real threat, understands what happened, responds correctly, and does so before the attacker can move. Humans still matter in that model. Autonomous security cannot become unaccountable security. The practical destination is a human-augmented autonomous SOC, where AI provides scale, correlation, and investigative speed while people retain judgment, governance, and control. Cybersecurity does look increasingly like AI’s third major product-market fit. But the larger opportunity isn’t just putting AI into more security products, but rather building a security architecture in which AI can finally make all of those products work together. Source: Tomasz Tunguz, “The Third Product-Market Fit in AI,” Oct. 26, 2026. San Jose, Calif. – Nov. 23, 2026

His point is about the growing role of AI across all five, but my takeaway is architectural, and goes a bit further. These functions increasingly need to work together.

AI Needs Evidence, Not More Data

Security teams already have enormous amounts of telemetry. From endpoints, networks, identities, firewalls, SaaS applications, cloud infrastructure, vulnerability scanners, and threat intelligence, the problem is certainly not just more data. The problem is turning that data into evidence that an analyst, or an AI system, can use to make a decision.

Consider a suspicious identity. To understand what actually happened, an investigation may need to connect an unusual login with workload access, endpoint activity, network behavior, vulnerabilities, and threat intelligence. If those signals remain trapped in different tools and data models, AI inherits the same problem analysts have struggled with for years: it has to reconstruct the attack one system at a time.

It means enabling AI to work across identity, endpoint, network, cloud, vulnerabilities, and threat intelligence as parts of the same investigation. This distinction will become more important as AI use grows. The future SOC should not be measured by how many models it runs, agents it deploys, or tokens it consumes. Humans still matter in that model. Autonomous security cannot become unaccountable security. The practical destination is a human-augmented autonomous SOC, where AI provides scale, correlation, and investigative speed while people retain judgment, governance, and control.

Cybersecurity does look increasingly like AI’s third major product-market fit.

But the larger opportunity isn’t just putting AI into more security products, but rather building a security architecture in which AI can finally make all of those products work together.

items.title: Kagi Mail Opens Its Public Beta at $99 a Year, Without End-to-End Encryption
items.summary: Kagi Mail is now open to anyone, and it isn’t end-to-end encrypted. Kagi, the company behind the paid, ad-free Kagi search engine and the Orion browser, announced the public beta on Monday. You can take a @kagimail.com address or bring your own domain, try it free for 60 days and then pay $99 a year or $9 a month, plus sales tax. It comes included with Kagi Ultimate, the $25-a-month top plan. The announcement promises “no surveillance, no ads, open standards, and no lock-in.” The word “encryption” doesn’t appear in it. The answer is in the FAQ on the product page : your mail is encrypted at rest and in transit, and there’s no end-to-end encryption or PGP, because Kagi Mail “has to read your mail to flag what needs you.” The launch drew more than 120 comments on Hacker News within a few hours, and encryption was one of the early questions there. As we published, the only other coverage came from forums and a few small tech sites.

items.title: Beyond the Alert: Compare, Correlate, and Optimize Digital Experience with ZDX Data Explorer

Broad organization-wide averages conceal regional edge cases, localized ISP degradation, and specific policy cohort friction. By pairing metric-based thresholding with deep hop-by-hop visibility and directional sorting, Data Explorer enables teams to benchmark trends across locations, ISPs, and user cohorts, helping them determine what to improve next and measure the real-world impact of their changes across their SASE journey from the device to the application. By applying direct numerical thresholds across chosen operational metrics, such as isolating sessions where Page Fetch Time (PFT) exceeds 1000 ms, ZDX Score drops below 65, or packet loss spikes during video meetings, teams strip away thousands of unimpacted data points to analyze underperforming cohorts.Filter by Egress and Intermediate ISP Hop IP Address: In a Zero Trust SASE deployment, user traffic traverses last-mile and intermediate ISPs before reaching Zscaler Public Service Edges (ZENs). Application latency frequently originates within an intermediary ISPs hop rather than the user's local connection or the security inspection engine. While traditional tools stop at the last-mile ISP, Data Explorer supports IP filtering across egress and intermediate ISPs correlated by app, region, and user cohorts, allowing teams to evaluate ISP reliability, performance bottlenecks, and direct-to-cloud path health over time.Isolate Faults in One View: Instantly rank grouped entities from High-to-Low or Low-to-High across selected metrics. Automated "Special Filters" dynamically surface the Top 10 or Worst 10 Geolocations and Zscaler Locations, allowing architects to immediately identify the most degraded regions during performance reviews, architecture planning, and postmortems. An L1 analyst opens ZDX Agent to investigate the active ticket queue.Root Cause Analysis & Resolution: ZDX Agent executes a targeted, deep-dive diagnosis on individual user sessions, analyzing client-side CPU usage, local Wi-Fi signal strength, and last-mile ISP latency. While initial user reports blamed local security policies, and identified the root cause as packet loss within an upstream Intermediate ISP hop. Frontline support can then assign the ticket to the network team.Global Correlation & Regional Discovery (Data Explorer): Run a multi-dimensional query to discover whether an issue extends across an entire region, ISP or key user cohort to drive strategic, organization-wide optimization.Setting the Analytical Baseline: A network architect opens Data Explorer and sets an evaluation window across eight active business hours to analyze cross-application collaboration metrics.Selecting Comparative Applications: Zoom and Teams are both selected to compare experience during the selected timeframe.Filtering by Experience Thresholds: To isolate degraded user sessions from healthy ones, the architect applies a metric filter for Mean Opinion Score (MOS) < 4 and Packet Loss >= 1%.Correlating User Cohorts and Carrier Transits: The architect filters by the Corporate Campus Egress IPs, groups the dataset by Intermediate ISP, and applies the Worst 10 Geolocations special filter. Schedule a personalized ZDX demo or explore more at zscaler.com/zdx.

items.title: Cleverbridge Confirms Attackers Copied Payment Card Data From Its Platform
items.summary: Cleverbridge confirms attackers stole payment card numbers, expiry dates and CVV codes, warning customers to watch for fraudulent transactions. Cleverbridge, which runs checkouts, payments and subscriptions for other companies, has confirmed that attackers copied payment card data from its platform. The company says it found the problem on 4 November and started notifying affected people on 20 November. That’s a gap of 16 days. “On 4 November 2026, Cleverbridge detected unauthorised activity in our platform and took immediate steps to contain the incident.” reads the incident update published by the company. “Whilst our investigation remains ongoing, regretfully, we have been able to determine that a third party copied payment card data stored on our platform.” Affected systems went offline for a short time and were back online the same day. Only later did the investigation show that a third party had copied payment card data stored on the platform, and the company says that the investigation is still running. The company’s website lists customers such as SUSE, Red Hat and Parallels, but the company has not said which businesses were affected. If you bought a product or service from a company that uses Cleverbridge, it may have handled your payment and stored your card details. Cleverbridge provides payment and subscription services to software and SaaS companies. Cleverbridge has not clearly explained what information was stolen on its public incident page. It says the exposed data may include payment card details and directs affected customers to check their individual notifications. However, a notification reviewed by BleepingComputer provides more details: the stolen information may include card numbers, expiration dates and CVV or CVC security codes. That last item is the one that matters. The card industry’s own rules generally bar companies from keeping the security code once a payment is authorised, so BleepingComputer asked Cleverbridge why the codes were accessible at all. The company did not disclose technical details about the attack, however, its answer excluded a ransomware attack. “None of our systems were encrypted.” continues the update. Cleverbridge says it hired TransUnion/Cyberscout, a third-party vendor, to support the notifications, and that a notice sent on its behalf is legitimate. It has offered credit or identity monitoring where available, with sign-up details in the notice. Asked why people weren’t told sooner, it says it moved fast and notified them without undue delay. Cleverbridge advises users to watch for phishing attempts and warns that it will never request card details, passwords or security codes by email, phone or text. “As always, we recommend that our users follow general best online security practices, remain vigilant, and be aware of phishing attempts.” the company states. “Out of an abundance of caution, please be cautious of unexpected emails, calls, or messages about this incident. Cleverbridge will never ask you for your card details, passwords, or security codes by email, phone, or text message. ” Call your card issuer sooner rather than later. Cleverbridge says the issuer may decide to replace your card after you report the incident. We recommend that you check your card statements carefully and tell your card issuer right away about any transaction that you do not recognise.” concludes the report. “You may also wish to contact your card issuer to tell them about this incident and follow any advice they give, as they may decide to replace your card. ” Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, payment card data)

items.title: How SASE Vendors Design their Solution - Part 5: Outage Survival—Does SASE Work When the Platform Dies?
items.summary: The Achilles' Heel of Cloud Services: Platform OutagesThe shift to cloud-delivered security introduces a new category of risk: platform outages. What happens to your organization’s security and connectivity if the SASE vendor's central management platform goes down? For many businesses, the internet is their corporate network, and a SASE outage can mean a complete corporate blackout.This is where one of the most critical architectural differentiators comes into play: the separation of the data plane and the control plane. A well-designed SASE platform is architected for SASE blackout resilience, ensuring that even a catastrophic failure of the central management infrastructure does not bring a customer's network to a halt. The Good: Strict Data Plane and Control Plane SeparationThe "good" design is one that maintains a strict separation between the Data Plane and the Control Plane.The Data Plane consists of the global network of enforcement nodes (POPs) that process and inspect live traffic. Its sole responsibility is to forward packets and apply security policies at line rate.The Control Plane is responsible for all management functions: the admin console, policy configuration, logging, and reporting.In a resilient architecture, the data plane is designed to operate autonomously. Each enforcement node maintains a local cache enforcement copy of the organization's security policies. If the control plane experiences a complete outage—meaning the admin UI is down, logs are not being processed, and policy changes cannot be made—the data plane continues to function without interruption. User traffic continues to flow, and the last known security policy continues to be enforced.This architectural principle of Data Plane Control Plane separation is the cornerstone of disaster recovery for SASE. It ensures that a vendor's management outage does not become their customer's network outage. The Ugly: A Tangled Mess of InterdependenciesIn contrast, many legacy SASE providers have architectures with dangerous interdependencies between their data and control planes. In these systems, the enforcement nodes may need to make real-time queries to the control plane to retrieve policy information, or the logging and data planes may be so tightly coupled that a failure in one can cascade and impact the other.This is the "ugly" design. If the central management or logging infrastructure fails, the data plane nodes can be left in a state of confusion. They may be unable to process new connections, or worse, they may fail-open, allowing traffic to bypass security inspection entirely. In the most severe cases, the entire service can go down, causing a total network outage for all customers.Furthermore, a resilient architecture extends to the endpoint agent. Smart agents should have automated agent failover mechanisms built in. They should be aware of multiple enforcement nodes and be able to automatically select a backup path if their primary node becomes unavailable. They should also have local bypass parameters that can be triggered as a last resort to maintain connectivity.For any organization evaluating a SASE vendor, the question of architectural resilience should be paramount. An outage is inevitable; how the platform survives it is a direct result of its design. A platform built with a strict separation of the data plane and control plane is one that is built for survival.

items.title: Microsoft Entra Connect Health Breach Exposes Tenant Metadata and Admin Details
items.summary: Microsoft Entra Connect Health breach exposed tenant metadata and admin details, potentially enabling targeted phishing and social-engineering attacks. Microsoft has disclosed a data breach involving its Entra Connect Health service, which exposed tenant metadata and administrator contact details. “On 9 November 2026, we detected a vulnerability in the Microsoft Entra Connect Health API that was introduced on 23 July 2026. The vulnerability could allow an unauthorized party to access tenant and service-monitoring metadata and potentially make changes to Connect Health monitoring configuration.” the company wrote on Reddit. Microsoft Entra Connect Health is a cloud service that helps administrators monitor the health, performance and alerts of their on-premises identity systems. The IT giant says no passwords, authentication tokens or valid cryptographic keys were compromised, but the exposed information could still help attackers craft convincing phishing and social-engineering attacks. The issue came from a vulnerability in the Entra Connect Health API, introduced on July 23, 2026. Microsoft identified the flaw on November 9 and deployed a server-side fix on November 19. “We deployed and fixed the vulnerability on 19 November 2026. On 20 November 2026, we concluded our investigation and determined that unauthorized read-only access to tenant-level metadata associated with your organization had occurred. We did not identify any unauthorized configuration changes.” the IT giant added. Customers do not need to install a software update because Microsoft addressed the problem on its side. The attackers could only view the data, but the exposure still created risks. They gained access to administrator email addresses, tenant IDs, domain names and synchronisation status. Attackers could use this information to plan targeted attacks and impersonate Microsoft support staff, service providers or internal IT administrators. Microsoft has not disclosed how many tenants were affected. However, several administrators and managed service providers have reported receiving notifications from the company, suggesting that the breach may have affected many customers. Microsoft says no software update or customer remediation is needed because the Entra Connect Health API vulnerability has been fixed. However, it recommends several precautionary steps. Organisations should alert security and IT teams to possible targeted phishing and social-engineering attempts, ensure administrator accounts use phishing-resistant MFA, and apply Privileged Identity Management for just-in-time access. They should also run Microsoft’s read-only PowerShell script to review potentially exposed metadata, check Connect Health settings, and examine Entra audit logs, sign-in logs and Azure Activity Logs for suspicious activity. Microsoft advises verifying the security notice directly through Azure Service Health rather than clicking email links. Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, Microsoft Entra Connect Health)

items.title: Prism Medical Products Data Breach Affects 1.3 Million Individuals
items.summary: North Carolina-based Prism Medical Products, LLC, a home medical supply provider acquired by the global healthcare distributor and solutions provider Henry Schein Inc. in January 2021, has announced a cybersecurity incident involving unauthorized access to patient data. The sensitive data of more than 1.3 million individuals was potentially compromised in the incident. According to its October 30, 2026, data breach notice, the incident was first identified on October 19, 2026, when suspicious activity was observed within certain parts of its network. Assisted by third-party cybersecurity experts, Prism Medical Products confirmed that an unauthorized third party accessed its network, and it appears that files containing patient information were obtained in the incident. Prism Medical Products said it took immediate steps to prevent further unauthorized access, including disabling remote access and changing credentials, and believes that those measures, along with additional security measures it has implemented, have ensured that its IT environment is safe and secure. Prism Medical Products did not state whether ransomware was used in the incident or if it received a ransom demand. A third-party vendor was engaged to review the affected data and confirmed that the data compromised in the incident includes names, addresses, phone numbers, and email addresses in combination with some or all of the following: medical and clinical information, health insurance information, payment and financial account information, and certain identifiers, such as Social Security numbers, driver’s license numbers, and other forms of government identifiers. Notification letters are now being mailed to the affected individuals, who have been offered 24 months of credit monitoring and dark web monitoring services. Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy While not mentioned by Prism Medical Products in its data breach notice, this appears to have been a cyberattack by a ransomware and data theft/extortion group called Wallstreet. The group first appeared in June 2026 and has targeted companies in multiple sectors, including healthcare, insurance, automotive, manufacturing, construction, government, and public sector firms. While the incident is not yet shown on the HHS’ Office for Civil Rights breach portal, the Oregon Attorney General was informed that the data breach affected 1,326,066 individuals.

items.title: Zero-day Flaw in Medical Imaging App Identified and Exploited AI Agents
items.summary: A zero-day vulnerability in an open-source AI-assisted medical imaging tool has been identified and exploited by an autonomous agentic AI platform. A threat actor linked to China is believed to be behind a series of attacks targeting educational institutions in East Asia (excluding mainland China) between September 8 and September 10, 2026. According to Amazon Threat Intelligence, which shared the findings of the investigation, the threat actor used a publicly hosted instance of Cairn, an open-source autonomous AI-based penetration testing framework, which was instructed to obtain shell access. Aside from configuring Cairn, the attack is believed to have had minimal human involvement. The AI-based pen testing tool used multiple AI agents to identify and exploit a zero-day vulnerability in the MONAI Label open-source medical imaging tool, which researchers use to speed up dataset annotation. It took 11 minutes to map the application’s API, identify a path traversal vulnerability, and exploit it to write files outside an intended storage directory. In a subsequent session, the agents wrote a Python reverse shell that automatically loads when Python starts and triggered an API endpoint to establish root access to the server. After the zero-day vulnerability was discovered, the threat actor stepped in and provided the agents with a proxy that tunnelled into a second university network, which was running the same vulnerable software. The researchers believe the threat actor used the same zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel, then instructed the agents to attack other devices on the network. Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Amazon Threat Intelligence discovered the campaign as the publicly hosted Carin instance used by the attackers was left exposed on the internet and could be accessed without authentication. Prompts were discovered to have been written in simplified Chinese, with timestamps in the executed scripts configured to China Standard Time. The vulnerability affects MONAI Label versions up to and including 0.8.5. The researchers notified the maintainers of MONAI Label, and the vulnerability will be fixed in version 0.5.6. The security advisory was published on GitHub on November 18, 2026, and contains workarounds for hardening security ahead of the release of the fixed version. The researchers warned that autonomous AI agents are already being used to find and exploit software vulnerabilities, and they can do it faster than security teams can react and triage a security alert. The researchers also describe an attempt by the AI agents to compromise a Redis target. The AI agents ran continuously for 16 hours and kept adapting, performing 148 sequential actions without any human involvement. “To keep pace, organizations should prioritize high-confidence detections that trigger automated response, with humans overseeing outcomes rather than reviewing every individual action,” suggest the researchers.

items.title: CrowdStrike buys missing network security piece in $43.9B Zscaler deal
items.summary: CrowdStrike agreed to acquire cloud security company Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal on Monday, combining endpoint protection with zero-trust network security in one of the largest cybersecurity acquisitions ever and intensifying the industry’s race to build broad security platforms. The deal brings together CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform, which focuses on endpoint, identity and cloud security, with Zscaler’s cloud-delivered network security and zero-trust access capabilities. CrowdStrike said the combined company is expected to begin with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR). The acquisition also addresses a strategic gap in CrowdStrike’s portfolio. While the company has expanded beyond endpoint protection into identity, cloud security and threat intelligence, Zscaler brings an established security service edge (SSE) and zero-trust network access platform. “With Zscaler, CrowdStrike will enter network security, cybersecurity’s largest single addressable market segment,” CrowdStrike said in a statement. The companies expect the deal to close in the second half of CrowdStrike’s fiscal 2028, subject to approval by Zscaler shareholders and regulators, the statement added. The deal is larger than Google’s $32 billion purchase of Wiz and Palo Alto Networks’ $25 billion acquisition of CyberArk , both completed earlier this year. From partnership to one platform CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz framed the deal around AI in the statement. “With Zscaler, we’re building cybersecurity’s operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely,” Kurtz said. Yih Khai Wong, research director at IDC, said the deal fits a pattern of larger security vendors “buying into adjacent control points rather than building them organically.” Until now, he said, CrowdStrike “lacks a strong, owned network/SSE layer.” The two companies are not starting from scratch. The statement described the relationship as one of CrowdStrike’s largest technology alliances, with more than 2,000 shared customers and 16 integrations. CrowdStrike argued that a partnership integrates separate products, while one company integrates “the data, the roadmap, the go-to-market, and the commercial model.” Wong said the existing partnership already delivers much of the correlation value. Ownership adds “control over the roadmap and the pace of integration,” he said. Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said the merger buys “fluency rather than new vocabulary.” One owner means a single data model and faster correlation, he said, but that gain is “narrower than any merger pitch will claim.” He advised CISOs to ask the vendors to show, in their own environments, which outcomes today’s integration cannot already reach. One contract, one renewal The commercial plan is central to the deal. After closing, customers of either company will be able to buy the other’s products on a single Falcon Flex contract, the statement said. CrowdStrike identified about 8,000 Zscaler customers that do not yet use CrowdStrike, and said it expects about $1 billion in annualized revenue synergies within 30 months of closing. “Falcon Flex will bring Zscaler onto the commercial model customers already use, so they commit once and expand from there,” the statement said. Gogia said that model shifts leverage over time. “Consolidation is sold at the first signature and priced at the second,” he said. The second signature comes at renewal, he said, when the supplier holds more of the estate and the buyer holds fewer alternatives. He advised CFOs and CISOs to price consolidation offers at their first full renewal, and to keep one credible alternative alive in each layer they consolidate. Wong said consolidation “addresses real integration challenges for enterprises that commit to a single platform, while quietly reducing the leverage and flexibility of those that don’t.” Enterprises in heavily regulated industries that need best-of-breed tools may find bundled platforms fall short, he added. Two layers, one release train CrowdStrike also expects $500 million in annualized cost synergies within 18 to 24 months of closing, mainly from optimizing data center infrastructure, vendors and operations, the statement said. For security teams, the question is whether that consolidation reaches the products themselves. Today the Falcon sensor and Zscaler’s client run as separate agents on separate clouds, with separate release schedules, Gogia said. “A merged agent, a shared update pipeline, or a single control plane would change that,” Gogia said. “One bad release would then reach the device and the way in together.” Wong said CISOs should build that scenario into their business continuity plans, since “an incident could affect both the endpoint agent and the access control plane.” Gogia advised teams to map every access rule that depends on CrowdStrike’s device posture check, and to keep a fallback route that relies on neither vendor. Customers that pair Zscaler with another endpoint product, or Falcon with another SSE provider, should get integration commitments in writing, he said. “Neutrality promised in a blog post lasts exactly as long as the blog post.” Until the deal closes, both companies will continue to operate independently, the statement added.

items.title: What Is a Proxy Server? How It Works and What It Doesn’t Hide
items.summary: A proxy server is a computer that contacts websites on your behalf. The sites see the proxy’s IP address, not yours. Most proxies cover a single app, usually the browser, and add no encryption of their own. That’s where a proxy parts ways with a VPN , which covers the whole device and encrypts everything up to its server. You probably use proxies already without calling them that. Schools and offices send web traffic through them, Opera’s free “VPN” is one, and so is the VPN built into Firefox since March 2026. Even this page took a detour on its way to you: privacyaffairs.com sits behind Cloudflare, which answers your browser in our server’s place. items.title: Bulgaria Discovers Massive Government Breach After Five Years of Undetected Spying
items.summary: Bulgaria uncovered a five-year cyberespionage campaign that stole 130GB of government files. The attacker and full impact remain unknown. Bulgaria ‘s ministry for innovation and digital transformation announced it had uncovered a hacking operation running since 2021. Reuters reports that more than 130 GB of documents, about 62 million pages, were downloaded from government databases over those five years. Minister Ivan Vassilev said there’s no evidence so far that Bulgarian citizens’ personal data was compromised. “The minister, Ivan Vassilev, said that since 2021 more than 130 GB, ​or 62 million pages, of documents had ​been downloaded, but that there was no evidence ⁠so far that Bulgarians’ personal data had been compromised, ​Nova TV reported on its website.” Reuters reports . The breach came to light only after Bulgaria introduced a new national cybersecurity monitoring system, which spotted suspicious activity in August. Until then, the country apparently had no system in place capable of detecting an intrusion that had been going on since 2021. This raises questions not only about the attackers’ capabilities but also about the lack of security monitoring inside government networks. Several international hacking groups may be behind the attack, but investigators haven’t linked it to any specific country or nation-state actor. The stolen files reportedly include cabinet documents, reports and communications between ministries and government agencies. “We discovered that several international hacker groups had accessed Bulgarian systems starting in 2021,” Vassilev said. “The information they stole included sensitive details of how Bulgarian state institutions operate” “At this stage, there is no evidence that the personal data of Bulgarian citizens has been affected,” the minister added. After the attack was discovered, several agencies joined the response, including intelligence services, the defense ministry, police, cybersecurity experts and international partners such as the EU’s cybersecurity agency. Authorities have isolated the affected systems, blocked the attackers’ access and removed the malware. Prosecutors have also been informed. Vassilev wants them to investigate not only the hackers but also whether government agencies failed to detect the intrusion earlier. The government also has questions to answer. Bulgaria went through several unstable governments and repeated elections during the five years the attackers remained inside its systems. This political instability may have affected long-term investment in cybersecurity. An attack that went unnoticed from 2021 to 2026 doesn’t only raise questions about the attackers’ skills. It also highlights how weak security monitoring allowed them to stay hidden for so long. This isn’t first time Bulgaria faced a major breach, and the contrast is worth noting. In 2019, hackers stole roughly 11 GB of data from the National Revenue Agency, exposing personal details on nearly five million citizens, about 71% of the population at the time, and a Russian link was floated before a 20-year-old local suspect was arrested. This time the target was institutional correspondence rather than citizen records, and the scale of documents taken, 130 GB against 11 GB, dwarfs that earlier case. What’s missing from Wednesday’s announcement is almost everything that would let the public judge the real damage: who did this, what specific documents went out the door, and whether any of it has already been used. Bulgaria’s own cybersecurity agency, BTA, described the find as “Government Uncovers Apparent Years-Long Breach of Administrative Networks”, language that tells you an investigation is still very much open, not closed. items.title: Meta Suspends DeFlock America Facebook Group, Citing Its “Dangerous Organizations” Rule
items.summary: Meta has suspended DeFlock America, the biggest Facebook group organizing against Flock Safety’s license plate cameras. The news came from Facebook user David Eduard, who posted a screenshot of Meta’s notice to the group’s admins on Sunday. Dated 21 November, it says Meta suspended the group because some of the activity on it “may not follow our rules,” and that this goes against its Community Standards on dangerous organizations and individuals. Eduard put the group at more than 840,000 members; IBTimes UK reported 818,000, Facebook’s own count, in late September. “Suspended for thought crimes,” Eduard wrote. By Monday his post had about 1,400 reactions and more than 500 shares, and the story had moved to Hacker News and Lemmy. We found no coverage by larger outlets as we published. When we tried to open the group on Monday while logged in to Facebook, it showed only the generic “This content isn’t available right now” page, which doesn’t give a reason. Meta hasn’t commented yet.

items.title: Clever AI prompt ideas every security leader should steal
items.summary: For all the talk of AI use by attackers and defenders, little attention is paid to ways CISOs and their security pros can leverage AI uniquely to expediate tasks, cut through the noise, facilitate decision-making, and potentially save big on auditing. Several specific AI prompts can help security leaders and staff handle multiple critical tasks not typically associated with AI for cyber defense, such as risk management, compliance, policy development, and critical thinking. Developing truly useful prompts isn’t particularly easy, however, because it often requires a significant amount of research and effort, not to mention lots of fine-tuning, which can take security teams away from other critical tasks. Fortunately, the security community is here to help, with advice on unique prompt ideas that have greatly aided them in strengthening security, facilitating decision-making, and saving time for hands-on defense. Create an adversarial assistant to control damage — and cut down AI slop Dzmitry Romanovadvocates establishing an AI prompt that acts as a second security reviewer to help catch latent problems before any damage occurs. The key, though, is to give it an adversarial twist so that it looks at a situation from the attacker’s perspective while critiquing the human security reviewer’s ideas. “What am I missing? What attack vectors or edge cases should I inspect?” is the kind of questions Romanov, cybersecurity team lead and senior security engineer at the Belarusian State University of Informatics and Radioelectronics and cybersecurity team lead with Vention, an AI-enabled software development company, such a prompt can help with. “This approach works most effectively when analyzing architecture or code, while reviewing penetration test results, and auditing cloud configurations, as well as when modeling threats and assessing risks,” Romanov says. Philippe Dourassov, AI pentest lead at Aikido Security, offers another version of the adversarial agent prompt — in this case against agent helpers. When agents are used to generate security reports, engineers often find themselves buried under irrelevant findings — noise, says Dourassov. However, when a second agent is deployed to analyze the quality of another agent’s work, and correct its output, the result can be surprisingly efficient. “The first agent has been given a task and will do everything it can to convince the humans that its results are relevant and critical, as this is what the agent would consider a good job,” Dourassov says, noting that his adversarial agent is basically a reviewer. “Its task is to eliminate noise, rectify claims, and highlight the true importance of the first agent’s result.” The agent’s definition of a good job, Dourassov says, is being able to eliminate noise and supply only signal to the human user. “Therefore, it’s essential to use an adversarial prompt to review agents’ output, so we ensure we don’t face security fatigue from AI slop.” Take care of business Brandyn Fisher, senior penetration testing technical lead at business and technology consulting firm Centric Consulting, offers three prompt ideas that CISOs can deploy on a regular basis to aid with their work. The first Fisher uses is a vendor due diligence prompt. “I feed it our organization’s risk thresholds and the vendor in question, and it benchmarks that vendor, sweeps the Internet for security pages, breach history, customer reviews, complaints, and recent news, then returns a structured report I can review and validate quickly,” he explains. Fisher also recommends crafting a professional writing prompt that takes technical analysis and reframes it into language a CIO or board will actually engage with. Gen AI pioneer Kevin Surace offered a similar prompt idea to attendees of this year’s CSO Conference and Awards in May. “Translate the SOC for the boardroom. This is important. They don’t really understand what’s going on,” Surace said. “The prompt here: ‘You are writing the cyber risk section of the board deck. You have four minutes of board time. Below is ninety days of security operations data. Produce three slides for a board that does not know what lateral movement means.’ This is so useful.” Fisher’s third prompt for CISOs is a tech debt reduction prompt “where I list our technology stack and have AI flag underutilized tools, overlapping capabilities, and consolidation opportunities,” he says. Fisher advises building each of his recommendations as a standing agent, project, or skill, or whatever your AI platform supports, so you have a static, repeatable spot to run it instead of rewriting the prompt from scratch every time. Don’t wait for a perfect first version, Fisher adds. “Get an initial prompt working, even if it’s rough, and have AI help draft the instructions themselves.” Expect to revise it several times before it’s reliable. Challenge your policies and content At the CSO Conference, Surace also highlighted how CISOs can use AI prompts to audit their policy libraries. “You are a compliance auditor. I am giving you our policy library and the current text of NIST CSF 2.0, ISO 27001:2022 Annex A, SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05, and the EU AI Act. Produce three lists,” his example prompt began, directing the LLM to find contradictions, gaps, and stale language — the kind of analysis big firms do for six figures in 12 weeks, he noted. Olivia Brännlund, CISO at Outpost24, a cybersecurity and risk management firm, regularly uses a similar prompt that turns AI into an internal auditor and security advisor. The tool reviews policy, processes, risk assessment, incident reports, contract clauses, and specific customer requirements. Brännlund believes that organizations that treat AI as an expert reviewer typically obtain more value than organizations that treat it as a content generator. The key, she states, “isn’t using AI to write content, but using it to challenge content.” Tying together policy review and the adversarial assistant concept, Surace advised CSO conference attendees to also “red team your own runbook.” “You are the operations lead for Scattered Spider. I am giving you our incident response playbook, our detection coverage matrix, and our on-call tree. Identify the five places this runbook fails,” his prompt started, probing for wrong assumptions, bottlenecks, escalation path weaknesses, and so on. “It’s totally worth doing this,” he said. “You will have more information in an hour than you, than you’ve ever had. Vet your agent’s capabilities and weaknesses Chris Hughes advises asking your model what your AI agents can actually do. “Give it an agent’s configuration, tool manifest, or MCP server definitions and ask it to summarize the agent’s effective permissions, the blast radius if it’s compromised, and whether a human approval step exists anywhere in the workflow,” says Hughes, who teaches in the CISO and Leading Enterprise Agentic AI Development Certificate Program at Carnegie Mellon University’s Heinz College. “Most organizations are deploying agents faster than they’re documenting what those agents can reach, and this closes the gap in minutes.” The model turns work that normally requires a senior architect into something an analyst can run at design review, before deployment, and after every change. It also surfaces assumptions the team stopped questioning, Hughes says. The model doesn’t share your blind spots, so it tends to flag the over-permissioned tool or the missing approval gate that everyone walked past, he notes. Once tuned, the prompt becomes a control in its own right rather than a one-off exercise. Embrace deep inspection Steve Tait, CTO at cloud security firm Skyhigh Security, suggests tailoring an AI prompt to take aim at AI prompts themselves, noting that perhaps the most important capability is a prompt response inspection that understands both data and intent. “CISOs should be able to determine not only whether sensitive information is entering or leaving an AI service, but whether a user or agent is attempting something risky—such as prompt injection, jailbreaks, policy evasion, credential exposure or unauthorized data access,” he says, adding that as AI agents become more common, that same inspection and policy model needs to extend beyond human prompts to agent-driven interactions. Tait believes that CISOs should think of prompt security as a platform control that needs to work across every major access path to AI, including Secure Web Gateway (SWG), zero trust network access, browser-based access, and APIs. “The goal should not be to plug a single gap for one AI application, but to establish a consistent policy and inspection layer wherever users or agents interact with AI services,” he explains. “This also means choosing an approach that can support hybrid environments, including organizations that still rely heavily on on-premises SWG infrastructure.”

items.summary: Back in 2017 I did some research into Oracle VirtualBox on Windows. Specifically I focussed on their mechanism to protect their VM processes from the user on the host. This time I found 3 new bypasses for protected processes, with an additional bug which was a broken fix for the 2020 bypass breaking due to changes in Windows. In this blog post I want to focus on one specific issue CVE-2026-87268 which abused a feature of the .NET Framework which, when combined with the implementation of the DLL loader hooks implemented by VirtualBox, permitted a bypass of the checks and allowed me to load arbitrary code into the protected process. Let’s dig into the root cause of the issue in .NET first, before moving on to exploitation in VirtualBox. ### .NET Assembly Loading The .NET Framework is interesting when it comes to bypassing process hardening as it supports loading assemblies from a memory buffer as long as you stick to only using managed code. This is obviously useful if the hardened process is maintained through verifying what DLLs can or cannot be loaded as it bypasses the traditional image mapping process. As the .NET runtime implementation is Microsoft signed, it’s usually permitted to load by any such checks. The canonical way to load from a memory buffer is to use the Assembly::Load static method which accepts a byte array. This does require you to run some .NET code first, or find a confused deputy to do the work for you. I used this API method to bypass VirtualBox process hardening back in 2017, I was able to get to the API through the JScript script engine, culminating in me releasing the generic DotNetToJScript tool. I’d always assumed this was the limit of bootstrapping arbitrary .NET from a memory buffer. If you tried to load a .NET assembly from a file it’d map it as an image section which would hit any DLL hardening checks and block an unsigned and untrusted binary from loading. However, in a “Doh” moment I realized I’d never verified this behavior to be true, thus I decided to take a look. The most important function to mapping a .NET assembly into memory seems to be `PEImageLayout::Map`, which is roughly the following in the version 4 of CLR.DLL which implements the runtime: ``` PEImageLayout *PEImageLayout::Map(HANDLE file) { PEImageLayout* image = new MappedImageLayout(file); if (!image->Image) { image = new FlatImageLayout(file); } if (image->Image) { if (!PEDecoder::CheckFormat(image->Image)) ThrowWin32(ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT); } return image; } ``` What is interesting is this code creates a `MappedImageLayout` object based on the file. If that fails it’ll fall back to using a different object, `FlatImageLayout`. The names kind of give away what they’re doing, but just to be sure let’s look at the implementations of the constructors: ``` void MappedImageLayout::MappedImageLayout(HANDLE file) { HANDLE mapping = CreateFileMapping(file, nullptr, SEC_IMAGE | PAGE_READONLY); if (mapping) { this->Image = CLRMapViewOfFileEx(mapping); } else { if (GetLastError() != ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT) ThrowLastError(); } DWORD policy = 0; if (EEConfig::EnforceCodeIntegrity() || (SUCCEEDED(WldpGetLockdownPolicy(nullptr, &policy, nullptr)) && !WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_OFF(policy) && !WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_CONFIG_CI(policy)) ) { ThrowWin32(ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT); } // ... } ``` The constructor for `MappedImageLayout` uses the CreateFileMapping API to convert the file handle into a section object. The code passes the `SEC_IMAGE` flag which instructs the kernel to assume the file is a PE executable and build an image section object including mapping in executable memory pages. Any protections which rely on verifying an image’s signature or location can be notified and take appropriate action. However if the `CreateFileMapping` call fails the code checks if the last error was not `ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT` and throws ending the load entirely. An additional check is made here to check if “Code Integrity” is enforced through the Windows Lockdown Policy (WLDP) APIs. This checks for the “Dynamic Code Security” code integrity policy being enabled or if a User Mode Code Integrity (UMCI) policy is enforced. If it is then an error is thrown ending the loading process. We’ll come back to this check when it becomes relevant. Assuming the mapping fails with the `ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT` error, then the loading process continues, creating a `FlatImageLayout` object instead: ``` void FlatImageLayout::FlatImageLayout(HANDLE file) { HANDLE mapping = CreateFileMapping(file, nullptr, PAGE_READONLY); if (mapping) { this->Image = CLRMapViewOfFileEx(mapping); } else { ThrowLastError(); } // ... } ``` This constructor is simpler, it just calls `CreateFileMapping` without the `SEC_IMAGE` flag. Therefore the file is mapped into memory as a data only section. There’s no executable pages, but that doesn’t matter for .NET. The final check, back in the first code snippet verifies that the PE file is valid with a call to `PEDecoder::CheckFormat`, throwing if it’s not valid. The take away from this is if we can get .NET to load a valid assembly file, but cause the first call to `CreateFileMapping` to fail with the `ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT` error we can get it to execute the file from memory. Any protection code which is expecting to check the loaded image section will not see the load and untrusted arbitrary code would be executed. Note this behavior only seems to work on .NET Framework v4, not the older .NET Framework such as v3.5 and v2. From what I can tell in the earlier frameworks, while this check can be bypassed in the same way and the `FlatImageLayout` object created, the runtime passes the assembly to the `LoadLibrary` API later in the loading process where it will fail to load. I didn’t spend much time checking if this was bypassable, as the older .NET Frameworks are no longer installed by default and aren’t even included as optional components in the latest versions of Windows 11. I also didn’t investigate the modern .NET runtimes, v5 and above for similar reasons. ### VirtualBox DLL Loading Hooks Now that we have a potential route to bypassing a process hardening image checker using .NET let’s dig into how it was exploitable in VirtualBox. The previous blog post described how VirtualBox on Windows adds hooks to the DLL loader in order to prevent untrusted images from loading into the process. The important hook for our purposes is the one attached to the `NtCreateSection` system call which is called under the hood by `CreateFileMapping` to create the image section object. The following is the start of the hook function: ``` NTSTATUS supR3HardenedMonitor_NtCreateSection(PHANDLE phSection, ACCESS_MASK fAccess, POBJECT_ATTRIBUTES pObjAttribs, PLARGE_INTEGER pcbSection, ULONG fProtect, ULONG fAttribs, HANDLE hFile) { bool const fExecProt = (fProtect & (PAGE_EXECUTE | PAGE_EXECUTE_READ | PAGE_EXECUTE_WRITECOPY | PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE)) != 0; if (hFile != NULL && hFile != INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) { bool const fImage = RT_BOOL(fAttribs & (SEC_IMAGE | SEC_PROTECTED_IMAGE)); bool const fExecMap = RT_BOOL(fAccess & SECTION_MAP_EXECUTE); if (fImage || fExecMap || fExecProt) { bool fCallRealApi; NTSTATUS rcNt = supR3HardenedScreenImage(hFile, fImage, true /*fIgnoreArch*/, &fAccess, &fProtect, &fCallRealApi, "NtCreateSection", true /*fAvoidWinVerifyTrust*/, NULL /*pfQuiet*/); if (!NT_SUCCESS(rcNt)) return rcNt; if (!fCallRealApi) return STATUS_TRUST_FAILURE; } } NTSTATUS rcNtReal = g_pfnNtCreateSectionReal(phSection, fAccess, pObjAttribs, pcbSection, fProtect, fAttribs, hFile); // ... ``` If the `NtCreateSection` call requests an executable section, such as via the `SEC_IMAGE` flag, then the file is passed to the `supR3HardenedScreenImage` support API which will check if the PE file matches VirtualBox’s loading criteria, only calling the original `NtCreateSection` system call if that succeeds or the file is not being mapped as executable. Importantly the `CreateFileMapping` call in `FlatImageLayout` would not hit the checks as it doesn’t request an image or executable mapping. In order for `CreateFileMapping` to set the `ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT` last error, `NtCreateSection` needs to return `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT`. We have two options for returning this status code, via the return code of `supR3HardenedScreenImage` or via the call to the original system call. Let’s see if the hardening code can even return this status code? ``` static NTSTATUS supR3HardenedScreenImageCalcStatus(int rc) { if (rc == VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH) return STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT; return STATUS_TRUST_FAILURE; } ``` It turns out that yes, the `supR3HardenedScreenImage` function can return this error code when mapping an internal error code to the status. Specifically if the error code is `VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH` then `supR3HardenedScreenImage` would return `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT`. Therefore, what sets `VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH`? This error is set in the PE parser implementation in VirtualBox, specifically in the `rtldrPEOpen` API. This is reachable via `RTLdrOpenWithReader` which is called by the `supHardenedWinVerifyImageByHandle` function which itself is called by `supR3HardenedScreenImage`. To cut a long story short, due to the way the parser is called the `VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH` error is returned if the architecture of the PE file doesn’t match the host architecture and yet the PE file contains executable sections. This turns out to be perfect, when you compile a managed code only .NET assembly as `AnyCPU,` it generates a 32-bit x86 PE file so that it can be run on any system. This is for compatibility, a 64-bit (or ARM64) Windows system can map 32-bit PE files as images, but vice versa is not guaranteed. However, as shown below in the output from the `dumpbin` utility there’s executable code in the file as indicated by the `size of code` field in the optional header. ``` C:\>dumpbin /headers DotNetAssembly.dll Microsoft (R) COFF/PE Dumper Version 14.44.35228.0 Copyright (C) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved. Dump of file DotNetAssembly.dll PE signature found File Type: DLL FILE HEADER VALUES 14C machine (x86) 3 number of sections D62E716A time date stamp 0 file pointer to symbol table 0 number of symbols E0 size of optional header 2022 characteristics Executable Application can handle large (>2GB) addresses DLL OPTIONAL HEADER VALUES 10B magic # (PE32) 48.00 linker version 35CC00 size of code 600 size of initialized data 0 size of uninitialized data ``` Therefore to force the image hardening checks to return `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT` all we need to do is compile any .NET assembly as `AnyCPU` and it’ll bypass VirtualBox’s image checks without messing with the file format. Crucially, because the .NET assembly DLL has not been modified, it remains a valid assembly which can be loaded by the `FlatImageLayout` class and thus get code execution. The final piece of the puzzle is how to get the assembly DLL loaded into VirtualBox? It’s not sufficient to just cause the DLL to be loaded via `LoadLibrary`, we need .NET to load the file as an assembly file. This is pretty easy to achieve via COM hijacking. We can write a .NET COM registration to the current user’s hive for a class we know a hardened VirtualBox process will load. Then start a VM, that will load the COM object, which loads the .NET runtime which finally loads our untrusted assembly. You can find a full PoC in the issue tracker. There is a small caveat, I haven’t mentioned the WLDP check yet. For VirtualBox this check is unlikely to matter, it will only apply if Windows has a configured code integrity policy which enables the `Dynamic Code Security` or the `UMCI` options. It’s possible a system could have such a policy which also grants VirtualBox’s own binaries to run but it seems unlikely. VirtualBox fixed the issue by never returning `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT` from the `supR3HardenedScreenImageCalcStatus` method. They also introduced some new code to make it more difficult to hijack COM objects by using an undocumented global option in COM to disable current user hive lookups. ### Attacking WDAC and Protected Processes If you’ve read this far you might be wondering if the .NET behavior applies to Windows Code Integrity enforcement in general. For example, both Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) and protected processes rely on the in-built code integrity mechanism to block untrusted DLLs from loading, are they vulnerable? Well yes, assuming you can find a way of forcing .NET to use the `FlatImageLayout` option by getting `NtCreateSection` to return `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT`. In VirtualBox this condition could be induced due to the behavior of the `NtCreateSection` hook on an unmodified .NET assembly file. For the built-in code integrity case there’s no user-mode hook to abuse, you only have the call to `NtCreateSection`. We need to be able to induce the `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT` status code from the system call without a) hitting the code integrity check first and b) the resulting image being invalid for .NET to load. The latter issue seemed to be most problematic, it’s likely that the signature validation would only run once the file was verified to be a valid PE image, but if we modify the file too much then .NET would refuse to load it. We can write a simple test harness to call `NtCreateSection` first with the file, then if that fails with `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT` call `Assembly::Load` passing the file path to load and see if that succeeds. From that you could write a fuzzer looking for a suitable modification, or just play with the file format manually. I found that it was almost trivial to create the right conditions. If you clear the `IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE` flag in the COFF File Header’s Characteristics flag field then `NtCreateSection` will fail to load the file as an image section, but it is ignored by .NET when loading the PE file. This single bit change is all you need to load an untrusted .NET assembly. This is when the WLDP check becomes important. If an enterprise is deploying a WDAC code integrity policy they have probably enabled `UMCI` or the `Dynamic Code Security` option which blocks this attack. The `Dynamic Code Security` option isn’t enabled by default, and as it disables all dynamic code loading in .NET including the byte array version of `Assembly::Load` it might result in breaking important applications. However, UMCI is one of the main reasons to deploy a WDAC policy as that restricts what user mode code is allowed to run. Still, I decided to try the attack against an installation of Windows 11 S Mode which does enable `UMCI` but doesn’t enable `Dynamic Code Security`. To test it out I needed force .NET to load the assembly file. For Windows 11 S Mode you can run many of the built-in .NET utilities which take assemblies on the command line. For example, the Assembly Registration Tool can be used to load a .NET assembly and call any register and unregister functions defined by the developer. For example, compile the following code as a .NET assembly adding your own code to `UnregisterFunction`: ``` using System; using System.Runtime.InteropServices; public class ComClass { [ComUnregisterFunction] public static void UnregisterFunction(Type t) { //Insert code here. } } ``` Modify the resulting assembly to remove the `IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE` flag. You don’t need to fix up anything else like the image checksum, a hex editor is all you need to change a single bit. Then you can pass the path to the modified assembly DLL to the RegAsm executable from the .NET runtime directory. Note, you should pass the `/unregister` option to run the `UnregisterFunction`, as unregistering doesn’t require administrator privileges. ``` C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET\Framework64\v4.0.30319\regasm.exe c:\path\to\assembly.dll /unregister ``` In theory this should have failed, but it didn’t. The modified assembly was loaded into memory and executed arbitrary code even with UMCI enabled. It turns out that the WLDP check is wrong, at least if only UMCI is enabled. It’s checking that the policy flags are not equal to the `WLDP_LOCKDOWN_CONFIG_CI` flag set, which represents: ``` WLDP_LOCKDOWN_DEFINED_FLAG | WLDP_LOCKDOWN_CONFIG_CI_FLAG | WLDP_LOCKDOWN_UMCIENFORCE_FLAG ``` Unfortunately this is exactly the flag setting returned by `WldpGetLockdownPolicy` on Windows 11 S Mode. Therefore the check passes and loading continues which then bypasses UMCI enforcement. For protected processes on a default installation of Windows the WLDP check doesn’t even come into play. Realistically, .NET should also check for protected status but it doesn’t. It should also be pointed out that you can only exploit Protected Process Light (PPL) processes. The original Protected Process (PP) requires DLLs to have page hashes in their authenticode signature, which the .NET runtime DLLs lack. Thus .NET fails to load, and we can’t reach the vulnerable code. For protected processes you can again abuse COM hijacking again. I found that `WerSecureFault.exe` loads a COM object during runtime, so by hijacking that registration and using the modified .NET DLL I could get arbitrary code as PPL at the TCB level without needing administrator privileges. ## Reporting to Microsoft Once I’d worked out how to abuse this behavior I wondered if it needs to be submitted to Microsoft for fixing. According to the MSRC Security Servicing Criteria any PPL bypass is not in scope. WDAC is a supported security boundary, however to quote the security goal, “Only executable code, including scripts run by enlightened Windows script hosts, that conforms to the device’s policy can run…” This could be interpreted as, if there is a policy that can be enabled to prevent the code from running, then it’s not eligible for fixing. I had assumed that the WLDP check was as designed and it was really the `Dynamic Code Policy` that was disabling this behavior. Therefore I decided not to report it, presenting it at the 2026 44Con conference instead. However, after discussing the issue with some .NET developers they were clear that although enabling `Dynamic Code Policy` blocked the bypass that was by accident and not the intended purpose of the policy. They asked me to submit it to MSRC. Unfortunately by this point, late September 2026, I’d already publicly disclosed therefore it was treated as a zero day, CVE-2026-108398, and was fixed in October 2026, less than a month after reporting. The fix was to correct the WLDP check to the following: ``` DWORD policy = 0; if (EEConfig::EnforceCodeIntegrity() || (SUCCEEDED(WldpGetLockdownPolicy(nullptr, &policy, nullptr)) && !WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_OFF(policy) && WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_ENFORCE(policy)) ) { ThrowWin32(ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT); } ``` The use of `WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_ENFORCE` specifically checks for UMCI being enabled and disabling loading from memory. However this wouldn’t change the behavior in PPL therefore that should still be bypassable. ## Conclusions As with my previous research into VirtualBox’s process hardening on Windows I was able to reuse the bypass to exploit the built in code integrity features of Windows. In this case the .NET code tried to adhere to policy but the developers just made a mistake. Unfortunately the behavior made me assume that it wouldn’t meet MSRC’s security servicing criteria and so the vulnerability wasn’t initially reported. While the criteria are useful, in cases like this where the expected behavior is unclear it can mean a real issue might not get reported. I’d like to thank the .NET team for getting a fix out so quickly.
