It turns out that yes, the `supR3HardenedScreenImage` function can return this error code when mapping an internal error code to the status. Specifically if the error code is `VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH` then `supR3HardenedScreenImage` would return `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT`. Therefore, what sets `VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH`?

This error is set in the PE parser implementation in VirtualBox, specifically in the `rtldrPEOpen` API. This is reachable via `RTLdrOpenWithReader` which is called by the `supHardenedWinVerifyImageByHandle` function which itself is called by `supR3HardenedScreenImage`.

To cut a long story short, due to the way the parser is called the `VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH` error is returned if the architecture of the PE file doesn’t match the host architecture and yet the PE file contains executable sections. This turns out to be perfect, when you compile a managed code only .NET assembly as `AnyCPU,` it generates a 32-bit x86 PE file so that it can be run on any system. This is for compatibility, a 64-bit (or ARM64) Windows system can map 32-bit PE files as images, but vice versa is not guaranteed. However, as shown below in the output from the `dumpbin` utility there’s executable code in the file as indicated by the `size of code` field in the optional header.

```
C:\>dumpbin /headers DotNetAssembly.dll Microsoft (R) COFF/PE Dumper Version 14.44.35228.0 Copyright (C) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved. Dump of file DotNetAssembly.dll PE signature found File Type: DLL FILE HEADER VALUES 14C machine (x86) 3 number of sections D62E716A time date stamp 0 file pointer to symbol table 0 number of symbols E0 size of optional header 2022 characteristics Executable Application can handle large (>2GB) addresses DLL OPTIONAL HEADER VALUES 10B magic # (PE32) 48.00 linker version 35CC00 size of code 600 size of initialized data 0 size of uninitialized data
```

Therefore to force the image hardening checks to return `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT` all we need to do is compile any .NET assembly as `AnyCPU` and it’ll bypass VirtualBox’s image checks without messing with the file format. Crucially, because the .NET assembly DLL has not been modified, it remains a valid assembly which can be loaded by the `FlatImageLayout` class and thus get code execution.

The final piece of the puzzle is how to get the assembly DLL loaded into VirtualBox? It’s not sufficient to just cause the DLL to be loaded via `LoadLibrary`, we need .NET to load the file as an assembly file. This is pretty easy to achieve via COM hijacking. We can write a .NET COM registration to the current user’s hive for a class we know a hardened VirtualBox process will load. Then start a VM, that will load the COM object, which loads the .NET runtime which finally loads our untrusted assembly. You can find a full PoC in the issue tracker.

There is a small caveat, I haven’t mentioned the WLDP check yet. For VirtualBox this check is unlikely to matter, it will only apply if Windows has a configured code integrity policy which enables the `Dynamic Code Security` or the `UMCI` options. It’s possible a system could have such a policy which also grants VirtualBox’s own binaries to run but it seems unlikely.

VirtualBox fixed the issue by never returning `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT` from the `supR3HardenedScreenImageCalcStatus` method. They also introduced some new code to make it more difficult to hijack COM objects by using an undocumented global option in COM to disable current user hive lookups.

### Attacking WDAC and Protected Processes

If you’ve read this far you might be wondering if the .NET behavior applies to Windows Code Integrity enforcement in general. For example, both Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) and protected processes rely on the in-built code integrity mechanism to block untrusted DLLs from loading, are they vulnerable?

Well yes, assuming you can find a way of forcing .NET to use the `FlatImageLayout` option by getting `NtCreateSection` to return `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT`. In VirtualBox this condition could be induced due to the behavior of the `NtCreateSection` hook on an unmodified .NET assembly file.

For the built-in code integrity case there’s no user-mode hook to abuse, you only have the call to `NtCreateSection`. We need to be able to induce the `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT` status code from the system call without a) hitting the code integrity check first and b) the resulting image being invalid for .NET to load. The latter issue seemed to be most problematic, it’s likely that the signature validation would only run once the file was verified to be a valid PE image, but if we modify the file too much then .NET would refuse to load it.

We can write a simple test harness to call `NtCreateSection` first with the file, then if that fails with `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT` call `Assembly::Load` passing the file path to load and see if that succeeds. From that you could write a fuzzer looking for a suitable modification, or just play with the file format manually.

I found that it was almost trivial to create the right conditions. If you clear the `IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE` flag in the COFF File Header’s Characteristics flag field then `NtCreateSection` will fail to load the file as an image section, but it is ignored by .NET when loading the PE file. This single bit change is all you need to load an untrusted .NET assembly.

This is when the WLDP check becomes important. If an enterprise is deploying a WDAC code integrity policy they have probably enabled `UMCI` or the `Dynamic Code Security` option which blocks this attack. The `Dynamic Code Security` option isn’t enabled by default, and as it disables all dynamic code loading in .NET including the byte array version of `Assembly::Load` it might result in breaking important applications.

However, UMCI is one of the main reasons to deploy a WDAC policy as that restricts what user mode code is allowed to run. Still, I decided to try the attack against an installation of Windows 11 S Mode which does enable `UMCI` but doesn’t enable `Dynamic Code Security`.

To test it out I needed force .NET to load the assembly file. For Windows 11 S Mode you can run many of the built-in .NET utilities which take assemblies on the command line. For example, the Assembly Registration Tool can be used to load a .NET assembly and call any register and unregister functions defined by the developer. For example, compile the following code as a .NET assembly adding your own code to `UnregisterFunction`:

```
using System; using System.Runtime.InteropServices; public class ComClass { [ComUnregisterFunction] public static void UnregisterFunction(Type t) { //Insert code here. } }
```

Modify the resulting assembly to remove the `IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE` flag. You don’t need to fix up anything else like the image checksum, a hex editor is all you need to change a single bit. Then you can pass the path to the modified assembly DLL to the RegAsm executable from the .NET runtime directory. Note, you should pass the `/unregister` option to run the `UnregisterFunction`, as unregistering doesn’t require administrator privileges.

```
C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET\Framework64\v4.0.30319\regasm.exe c:\path\to\assembly.dll /unregister
```

In theory this should have failed, but it didn’t. The modified assembly was loaded into memory and executed arbitrary code even with UMCI enabled. It turns out that the WLDP check is wrong, at least if only UMCI is enabled. It’s checking that the policy flags are not equal to the `WLDP_LOCKDOWN_CONFIG_CI` flag set, which represents:

```
WLDP_LOCKDOWN_DEFINED_FLAG | WLDP_LOCKDOWN_CONFIG_CI_FLAG | WLDP_LOCKDOWN_UMCIENFORCE_FLAG
```

Unfortunately this is exactly the flag setting returned by `WldpGetLockdownPolicy` on Windows 11 S Mode. Therefore the check passes and loading continues which then bypasses UMCI enforcement.

For protected processes on a default installation of Windows the WLDP check doesn’t even come into play. Realistically, .NET should also check for protected status but it doesn’t. It should also be pointed out that you can only exploit Protected Process Light (PPL) processes. The original Protected Process (PP) requires DLLs to have page hashes in their authenticode signature, which the .NET runtime DLLs lack. Thus .NET fails to load, and we can’t reach the vulnerable code.

For protected processes you can again abuse COM hijacking again. I found that `WerSecureFault.exe` loads a COM object during runtime, so by hijacking that registration and using the modified .NET DLL I could get arbitrary code as PPL at the TCB level without needing administrator privileges.

## Reporting to Microsoft

Once I’d worked out how to abuse this behavior I wondered if it needs to be submitted to Microsoft for fixing. According to the MSRC Security Servicing Criteria any PPL bypass is not in scope. WDAC is a supported security boundary, however to quote the security goal, “Only executable code, including scripts run by enlightened Windows script hosts, that conforms to the device’s policy can run…” This could be interpreted as, if there is a policy that can be enabled to prevent the code from running, then it’s not eligible for fixing.

I had assumed that the WLDP check was as designed and it was really the `Dynamic Code Policy` that was disabling this behavior. Therefore I decided not to report it, presenting it at the 2026 44Con conference instead.

However, after discussing the issue with some .NET developers they were clear that although enabling `Dynamic Code Policy` blocked the bypass that was by accident and not the intended purpose of the policy. They asked me to submit it to MSRC. Unfortunately by this point, late September 2026, I’d already publicly disclosed therefore it was treated as a zero day, CVE-2026-108398, and was fixed in October 2026, less than a month after reporting.

The fix was to correct the WLDP check to the following:

```
DWORD policy = 0; if (EEConfig::EnforceCodeIntegrity() || (SUCCEEDED(WldpGetLockdownPolicy(nullptr, &policy, nullptr)) && !WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_OFF(policy) && WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_ENFORCE(policy)) ) { ThrowWin32(ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT); }
```

The use of `WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_ENFORCE` specifically checks for UMCI being enabled and disabling loading from memory. However this wouldn’t change the behavior in PPL therefore that should still be bypassable.

## Conclusions

As with my previous research into VirtualBox’s process hardening on Windows I was able to reuse the bypass to exploit the built in code integrity features of Windows. In this case the .NET code tried to adhere to policy but the developers just made a mistake.

Unfortunately the behavior made me assume that it wouldn’t meet MSRC’s security servicing criteria and so the vulnerability wasn’t initially reported. While the criteria are useful, in cases like this where the expected behavior is unclear it can mean a real issue might not get reported. I’d like to thank the .NET team for getting a fix out so quickly.

items.title: BADBOX 3.0 Exposed: Massive Botnet Hides Ad Fraud Inside Android TV Boxes
items.summary: BADBOX 3.0 returns with 40 billion daily ad requests, turning infected TV boxes into fraud machines The BADBOX botnet is back, and its latest version has reached a scale that makes previous ad fraud operations look relatively small. Researchers from HUMAN’s Satori Threat Intelligence and Research team have uncovered BADBOX 3.0, a large-scale operation that uses infected Android-based TV boxes and other low-cost consumer devices to generate billions of fraudulent advertising requests every day. “At its height, BADBOX 3.0 accounted for roughly 40 billion bid requests a day and more than 4% of all CTV traffic observed by the Human Defense Platform. BADBOX 3.0’s volume was more than three times the volume of the previous record holder , VASTFLUX, and represents a larger peak than the last five years’ worth of published Satori investigations combined .” reads the report published by Human. “BADBOX 3.0 runs primarily on low-cost consumer devices infected with new backdoors that deliver fraud modules, including some that HUMAN researchers recognized from BADBOX and BADBOX 2.0 .” According to the investigation, the operation peaked at around 40 billion bid requests per day, accounting for more than 4% of all connected TV (CTV) traffic observed by HUMAN’s Defense Platform. That’s more than three times the volume attributed to VASTFLUX , the previous record holder. The latest findings show that the operators haven’t simply rebuilt the previous botnet. They’ve expanded its capabilities by combining advertising fraud with the abuse of residential proxy networks, using the same compromised devices for both activities. “The investigation began with a backdoor packaged as a system application with two hardcoded endpoints.” continues the report. “One endpoint retrieves the list of modules to load in the background, and the second handles logging.” BADBOX 3.0 primarily targets inexpensive, off-brand Android devices, including TV boxes, smartphones and tablets running the Android Open Source Project (AOSP). Some of these devices reportedly arrive with backdoors already installed, allowing attackers to gain privileged access and install additional malicious components. The advertising fraud works by running video ads in hidden windows. The infected device plays the ads in the background, while the malware generates advertising requests that impersonate legitimate connected TV applications. Advertisers and advertising platforms therefore receive what appears to be genuine traffic from popular streaming services, even though the applications being impersonated aren’t actually running on the infected devices. “Modules delivered through BADBOX 3.0 mimic video ad software development kits (SDKs) and render the ads in a hidden window, so the ad plays on the device while the screen shows nothing unusual.” HUMAN researchers report. “The resulting bid requests present themselves as coming from well-known, legitimate CTV apps that the threat actors impersonated to route their traffic. “ The investigation also uncovered another revenue stream. The malware silently enrolls infected devices in residential proxy networks, turning their owners’ internet connections into infrastructure that third parties can rent and use. Researchers identified 11 such networks, including ten commercially available services and PXYEDGE, a network allegedly operated by the same threat actors behind the BADBOX campaigns. “One of those networks is PXYEDGE, the rebranded successor to the IpMoYu network exposed in BADBOX 2.0.” the report states. “Not all of the operation’s ad fraud requires an infected device: HUMAN also observed spoofed server-side ad insertion (SSAI) traffic monetized through many of the same supply paths.” The device owner unknowingly provides the bandwidth and residential IP address, while someone else monetizes that access. This creates a problem that extends beyond advertising fraud. Residential proxies can help criminals conceal the origin of their activities, making it harder to identify attacks involving account takeovers, fake account creation, payment card fraud and other forms of abuse. The report also establishes a connection between PXYEDGE and IpMoYu, the residential proxy network previously exposed during the BADBOX 2.0 investigation. Researchers found overlapping infrastructure, proxy modules and task servers, concluding that PXYEDGE is likely IpMoYu operating under a different name. They also observed approximately 340,000 unique connections across monitored services, while the network advertised around 200,000 available nodes. “The eleventh network is PXYEDGE , operated by the threat actors themselves and described below.” Human states. “Enrolling a device in these networks turns the owner’s home internet connection into a commodity without their knowledge or consent. The device owner pays for the bandwidth, and someone else sells access to the address. “ Another important finding concerns the infrastructure behind the operation. Satori researchers linked the BADBOX 3.0 malware catalog to TXCZ, a Chinese electronics manufacturer, through several independent technical connections. These include command-and-control infrastructure, manufacturer-owned domains, preinstalled software, device-specific checks embedded in the malware and public code repositories used to distribute malicious modules. Researchers also identified a repository account incorporating TXCZ’s name and linked its maintainer to the threat activity. These findings establish several connections between the malware infrastructure and the manufacturer. They don’t, by themselves, establish the extent of the company’s knowledge or involvement in the criminal operation. The operators have also taken steps to make the botnet harder to disrupt. Instead of relying on a single download location, they distribute malicious modules through public code repositories and multiple backup hosting services. Some payloads are mirrored through an open-source content delivery network, while a self-hosted GitHub proxy helps devices retrieve files even when access to the original repositories is blocked. This approach also gives researchers visibility into the malware’s development. By examining repository histories, Satori identified an actively maintained catalog containing hundreds of module versions, including components associated with earlier BADBOX campaigns and the vo1d malware family. BADBOX has survived previous disruption efforts. Researchers first discovered the malware in 2023, when they found low-cost Android devices with a backdoor already installed in their firmware. In 2025, they uncovered BADBOX 2.0, a much larger operation that had infected more than 10 million devices across 222 countries and territories. Google, HUMAN, Trend Micro, Shadowserver and other partners then worked together to disrupt it. However, as BleepingComputer reports, the operators have returned with a new version. HUMAN also joined a separate operation led by Google to disrupt XCPE, a related but different malware campaign. Researchers found more than one million infected devices in over 200 countries and territories. The operation also helped identify and take down several command-and-control domains used by BADBOX 3.0. The researchers stress that disrupting the infrastructure doesn’t necessarily eliminate the threat. Previous investigations showed that the operators could rebuild their capabilities by moving to new servers, changing distribution methods and adapting their malware. For consumers, the advice remains straightforward: buy devices from reputable manufacturers, check that Android devices are Play Protect certified, and install applications only through official marketplaces. Cheap, uncertified Android TV boxes deserve particular scrutiny, especially when their software and manufacturer cannot be independently verified. The most important lesson from BADBOX 3.0 is that a consumer device can become part of a criminal operation without its owner noticing anything unusual. It can generate fraudulent advertising revenue, provide access to a residential internet connection and help conceal other malicious activities. The problem isn’t limited to the money lost by advertisers. It’s also about consumers unknowingly providing the infrastructure criminals need to operate. “Each chapter of this research has ended with a version of the same observation: disrupting an operation and dismantling the conditions that produced it are different achievements.” the report concludes. “BADBOX 3.0 shows what that intact supply chain produces. The capability now lives in public code repositories, mirrored across hosting platforms, a mainstream CDN, and a proxy built to slip past network blocks, with fallback locations written into every module record. Its proxy network survived exposure by changing its name. Its ad fraud, hidden on the devices and passed off under the names of legitimate apps, reached a daily volume larger than any ad fraud operation disclosed before it.” Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, newsletter)

items.title: Bromcom - 355,051 breached accounts
items.summary: In September 2026, UK education software provider Bromcom suffered a data breach involving a legacy single sign-on (SSO) registration system . The incident exposed 355k unique email addresses belonging to staff and pupils at UK schools, alongside SSO registration reference numbers. Bromcom confirmed that no passwords or authentication tokens were exposed, and that the incident did not enable access to Microsoft or Google accounts or its school management system.

items.title: Spain Stops NoName057(16) From Getting a Physical Foothold
items.summary: Spanish police arrested the alleged leader of NoName057(16) ‘s first physical cell in Spain, seizing weapons, ammunition and crypto wallets. Spain’s National Police arrested a man in Burgos last Tuesday, calling him the main instigator behind what would have been NoName057(16)’s first physical cell in the country. “The arrested man carried out propaganda, glorification and recruitment activities in favor of NoName057(16), and disseminated calls on social networks to cyberattack state institutions and confront the police.” reads the announcement published by the Spanish Police. “This group claimed that the propaganda campaign it carried out in eight locations in Castile and León, Aragon, La Rioja and Madrid was the work of “its volunteers”.” Until now, the pro-Russian group’s operations had been limited to cyberattacks. Spanish police say the arrest stopped plans to start violent activities. The suspect is being held on charges of belonging to a cyberterrorist organization and promoting terrorism. “His arrest has thus far thwarted the start of violent attacks. This organization is believed to be responsible for at least 447 cyberattacks in Spain since 2014 against institutions, banks, and transport companies.” continues the announcement. “The arrested individual carried out propaganda, glorification, and recruitment activities on behalf of NoName057(16), and disseminated calls on social media to cyberattack state institutions or confront the police. He also acted as an intermediary for recruiting new supporters and referred interested parties to a recruitment system linked to NoName057(16). “ A search of his home uncovered much more than computer equipment. Police seized a semi-automatic rifle with a folding stock, several carbines and shotguns, high-capacity magazines, and more than 5,000 rounds of ammunition, including military-grade ammunition. Officers also found homemade clubs fitted with screws, double-edged detachable spears, brass knuckles, illegal pepper spray, chemical containers, and ten canisters of butanol. The discovery suggests that the suspect may have been preparing for activities beyond cyberattacks. “The arrested man progressed from participating in online conspiracy groups to actively engaging in a channel where he promoted and glorified the group’s actions.” continues the report. “Last year, he distributed stickers bearing the organization’s emblem and QR codes that linked to its official channels in Burgos, Palencia, Lerma, Valladolid, Zaragoza, Logroño, Aranda de Duero, and Madrid.” NoName057(16) isn’t a new name to Spanish authorities. The group has claimed at least 447 cyberattacks in the country since 2024, hitting institutions, banks, and transport companies. It formed in March 2022, shortly after Russia invaded Ukraine, with NATO members, the EU, and other Western allies as its stated targets. The arrested man wasn’t directly involved in carrying out cyberattacks. Instead, he used social media to encourage attacks against government institutions and calls for confrontations with police. He also helped recruit new members by directing interested people to the group’s official recruitment system. In addition, he spread the group’s propaganda in eight locations across Castile and León, Aragon, La Rioja, and Madrid, handing out stickers with its logo and QR codes linking to its online channels. Investigators say he gradually moved from following online conspiracy groups to running his own channel, where he praised the group’s activities. A court released him under certain conditions while the investigation continues. Police also found three physical cryptocurrency wallets containing bitcoin and are still investigating the origin of the funds. The timing isn’t a coincidence on the political side either. On 16 November, the Council of the European Union sanctioned NoName057(16) under its cyberattack sanctions regime, freezing its funds and banning anyone from making resources available to it. A government can freeze an accounts and still not stop someone from stockpiling ammunition in Burgos, which is exactly the gap this arrest closes. The case also lands days after Spanish courts ordered a full shutdown of the neo-Nazi group National Nucleus, sealing its headquarters in Burgos, Valladolid, and Madrid. Two unrelated extremist networks, one city, two closures in the same week. For a hacktivist group whose previous reach never left a browser tab, this represents the organization’s “first consolidated physical presence” in Spain. “The arrested man carried out propaganda, glorification and recruitment activities in favor of NoName057(16), and disseminated calls on social networks to cyberattack state institutions and confront the police.” reads the announcement published by the Spanish Police.

“This group claimed that the propaganda campaign it carried out in eight locations in Castile and León, Aragon, La Rioja and Madrid was the work of “its volunteers”.”

Until now, the pro-Russian group’s operations had been limited to cyberattacks. Spanish police say the arrest stopped plans to start violent activities. The suspect is being held on charges of belonging to a cyberterrorist organization and promoting terrorism.

“His arrest has thus far thwarted the start of violent attacks. This organization is believed to be responsible for at least 447 cyberattacks in Spain since 2014 against institutions, banks, and transport companies.” continues the announcement. “The arrested individual carried out propaganda, glorification, and recruitment activities on behalf of NoName057(16), and disseminated calls on social media to cyberattack state institutions or confront the police. He also acted as an intermediary for recruiting new supporters and referred interested parties to a recruitment system linked to NoName057(16). “

A search of his home uncovered much more than computer equipment. Police seized a semi-automatic rifle with a folding stock, several carbines and shotguns, high-capacity magazines, and more than 5,000 rounds of ammunition, including military-grade ammunition. Officers also found homemade clubs fitted with screws, double-edged detachable spears, brass knuckles, illegal pepper spray, chemical containers, and ten canisters of butanol. The discovery suggests that the suspect may have been preparing for activities beyond cyberattacks.

“The arrested man progressed from participating in online conspiracy groups to actively engaging in a channel where he promoted and glorified the group’s actions.” continues the report. “Last year, he distributed stickers bearing the organization’s emblem and QR codes that linked to its official channels in Burgos, Palencia, Lerma, Valladolid, Zaragoza, Logroño, Aranda de Duero, and Madrid.”

NoName057(16) isn’t a new name to Spanish authorities. The group has claimed at least 447 cyberattacks in the country since 2024, hitting institutions, banks, and transport companies. It formed in March 2022, shortly after Russia invaded Ukraine, with NATO members, the EU, and other Western allies as its stated targets.

The arrested man wasn’t directly involved in carrying out cyberattacks. Instead, he used social media to encourage attacks against government institutions and calls for confrontations with police. He also helped recruit new members by directing interested people to the group’s official recruitment system. In addition, he spread the group’s propaganda in eight locations across Castile and León, Aragon, La Rioja, and Madrid, handing out stickers with its logo and QR codes linking to its online channels.

Investigators say he gradually moved from following online conspiracy groups to running his own channel, where he praised the group’s activities. A court released him under certain conditions while the investigation continues. Police also found three physical cryptocurrency wallets containing bitcoin and are still investigating the origin of the funds.

The timing isn’t a coincidence on the political side either. On 16 November, the Council of the European Union sanctioned NoName057(16) under its cyberattack sanctions regime, freezing its funds and banning anyone from making resources available to it. A government can freeze an accounts and still not stop someone from stockpiling ammunition in Burgos, which is exactly the gap this arrest closes.

The case also lands days after Spanish courts ordered a full shutdown of the neo-Nazi group National Nucleus, sealing its headquarters in Burgos, Valladolid, and Madrid. Two unrelated extremist networks, one city, two closures in the same week. For a hacktivist group whose previous reach never left a browser tab, this represents the organization’s “first consolidated physical presence” in Spain.

What are threat intelligence feeds?
items.summary: What are threat intelligence feeds, and why do they matter for your cyber defenses? These real-time data streams are vital for pre-empting cyberattacks, providing the latest information on potential threats. By informing you of dangers before they strike, threat intelligence feeds are your first line of digital defense.
items.summary_html:
What are threat intelligence feeds, and why do they matter for your cyber defenses? These real-time data streams are vital for pre-empting cyberattacks, providing the latest information on potential threats.

By informing you of dangers before they strike, threat intelligence feeds are your first line of digital defense. This article will explore their types, impacts, and integration with your cybersecurity measures.

Key takeaways
  • Threat intelligence feeds provide real-time data on cyber threats, enabling security teams to quickly identify, understand, and mitigate threats by offering actionable intelligence including IOCs, TTPs, and context for the most pressing issues.
  • Through proactive threat detection and response, threat intelligence feeds are integral to enhancing an organization’s security posture, ensuring early identification and mitigation of threats, thereby helping develop refined defensive strategies and improve decision-making.
  • Effective use of threat intelligence feeds involves integrating them with an organization’s existing security tools and infrastructure, prioritizing threats to allocate resources efficiently, and continuously evaluating them to maintain quality, reliability, and cost-effectiveness.
Breaking down threat intelligence feeds

Threat intelligence feeds provide a constant flow of data that offers up-to-the-minute details about cyber threats worldwide. These feeds gather information from various sources, including security experts, government agencies, and open-source intelligence.

The data is processed and analyzed, transforming raw information into actionable threat intelligence. This actionable intelligence includes indicators of compromise (IOCs), tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) used by threat actors. This threat intel is invaluable to security teams, enabling them to identify, understand, and mitigate threats swiftly.

Moreover, threat intel feeds play a pivotal role by providing automated streams of useful threat information, including indicators of compromise (IoCs), information on threat actors, suspicious domains and IP addresses, malware hashes, and more, which are essential for maintaining an organization’s security posture.

TechTarget highlights the value of threat intel feeds by stating:

“Any serious effort to interrupt cyberthreats should incorporate threat intelligence.”

And as Cloudflare warns:

“Organizations that are set up to block last year’s attacks may be compromised by this year’s attack tactics.”

The effectiveness and utility of threat intelligence feeds rely on the context they offer. Without context, the data might seem overwhelming and challenging to interpret. However, with the right context, security teams can focus on the most pressing threats, thus enhancing their response time and efficiency.

What are the key components of threat intelligence feeds?

Effective threat intelligence feeds share common attributes. They offer:

  • Real-time updates: ensuring quick incident response and timely adjustments to security policies
  • A proven track record of accuracy: outdated or incorrect information can compromise security efforts, making accuracy a crucial component
  • Relevance to either incident response or strategic planning: often determined by whether it offers real-time insights versus long-term trends.

Contextual analysis in threat intelligence feeds is another key component. It provides insights into the origins and impact of threats, aiding security teams in crafting appropriate response and mitigation strategies. Furthermore, effective threat intel feeds must present relevant data, streamlining security investigation and response. This curation saves valuable time for security teams.

Finally, the quality and industry relevance of the sources contributing to threat intelligence feeds are vital to the utility and effectiveness of the received intelligence.

What are the four types of threat intelligence feeds?

Threat intelligence feeds are primarily categorized into four types:

  • Commercial feeds: These collect anonymized customer metadata and analyze it to provide threat intelligence. They often come from reputable cybersecurity firms and provide comprehensive coverage of the threat landscape.
  • Open-source feeds: These are publicly available sources of threat intelligence, such as public forums, blogs, newsletters , social media, and even threat intelligence browser extensions. They can provide valuable information but may require more manual threat intelligence analysis.
  • Community-based feeds: These are collaborative efforts where individuals and organizations share threat intelligence with each other. They can be valuable for niche or specific threat information.
  • Government and Non-Governmental Organization (NGO) Threat Intelligence Feeds: governments and NGOs provide threat intelligence feeds, sometimes for free or at a cost, which include platforms for sharing threat data among entities, like the Department of Homeland Security’s Automated Indicator Sharing or the FBI’s InfraGard project. These feeds are valuable for staying informed about cyber threats but relying solely on them can result in a limited perspective of the threat landscape.

Each type has its unique characteristics and advantages.

Why are cyber threat intel feeds important?

Threat intelligence feeds play a pivotal role in transforming reactive security efforts into proactive ones. By providing real-time insights into potential cyberattacks, these feeds enable early identification and response, thereby preventing breaches.

The information these feeds offer enhances the ability of security teams to:

  • Develop refined defensive strategies
  • Gain insights into the tactics, techniques, and procedures of adversaries
  • Create a clear picture of the threat landscape

Furthermore, threat feeds empower security teams to make faster and more informed decisions, backed by data. This data-driven approach significantly bolsters an organization’s cybersecurity. With a broader understanding of the cyber threat landscape, organizations can better assess and prioritize risks, ensuring resources are allocated to the most pressing ones.

Enhancing security posture

One of the significant benefits of threat feeds is their capacity to enhance an organization’s security posture. By offering actionable intelligence, these feeds empower security teams to gain a deeper understanding of threats and fine-tune their protection strategies. However, to fully harness the power of these feeds, organizations need to evaluate their existing security posture, understand their industry’s inherent risks, and consider the compatibility of the feeds with their current security tools.

An effective way to improve response times to cyber threats is through security automation. By automating responses to alerts from threat intelligence feeds, organizations can act swiftly against cyber threats, thereby preventing potential data breaches.

Proactive threat detection and response

Threat intelligence feeds are the cornerstone of proactive threat detection and response. They enable security teams to:

  • Address security threats before they escalate into major issues
  • Proactively identify and mitigate threats
  • Understand the tactics used by threat actors
  • Guide security policies
  • Identify vulnerabilities
  • Inform access permissions and security updates

Cybersecurity professionals utilize threat intel to stay one step ahead of potential cybersecurity threats and protect their systems and data.

Threat intelligence feeds provide essential information on emerging threats and share best practices for responding, which significantly supports incident response efforts. With real-time threat data, security teams are promptly informed of potential issues, reducing the likelihood and costs of significant data breaches.

Where threat intelligence data comes in

Leveraging threat intelligence data effectively is a critical process that involves integrating feeds into existing security tools and prioritizing threats to allocate resources efficiently. The actionability of threat intelligence data is determined by the level of context provided and its capacity to be readily used in correlation with other security tools and platforms.

Curated threat intel feeds compile data from various sources, including public and private repositories, allowing security teams to save time and enhance their investigative and response efforts.

Integration with security tools

Integrating threat intel feeds with existing security tools can:

  • Extend these tools’ useful life
  • Improve their return on investment
  • Minimize alert fatigue in security operations centers
  • Provide filtered, prioritized alerts for better management
  • Incorporate both third-party and local threat intelligence into existing security solutions
  • Expand the slate of covered threats
  • Enhance the identification and blocking of threats

Advanced Threat Intelligence (ATI) tools that employ algorithms to rapidly identify anomalies often assist in this integration. The process is further supported by the availability of integrations such as APIs or native third-party integrations that simplify ingestion into the current security infrastructure.

Prioritizing threats and allocating resources

Threat intelligence data facilitates the creation of metrics that help organizations quantify and rank threats. This process effectively prioritizes critical vulnerabilities, ensuring resources are allocated to the most pressing threats. Classifying high-risk activities and incidents using threat intelligence data supports the strategic allocation of cybersecurity resources and enhances strategic threat intelligence.

Incorporating threat intelligence into incident response mechanisms allows organizations to:

  • Respond to threats both swiftly and strategically
  • Strategize the deployment of rules and Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) in Security Operations Centers (SOCs)
  • Ensure that rules and IoCs are constantly updated and fine-tuned to keep up with evolving threats.

Threat intelligence feeds also provide vital data on vulnerabilities, exploits, and attack methods, which can be prioritized to improve patch management efforts within an organization.

How can I choose the right threat intelligence feed for my organization?

Choosing the right threat intelligence feed for your organization is a critical decision. It involves assessing quality, reliability, cost, and value, as well as considering the organization’s specific needs and budget constraints.

Criteria for evaluating threat intelligence feeds include the ability to:

  • update data in real time
  • access to multiple data sources
  • and the speed and format of the feed’s dissemination

To enhance the value of threat intelligence within an organization, it is important to evaluate the unique data each feed provides to prevent overlapping information and redundancy.

Integrating threat intelligence feeds requires analyzing their relevance to the organization’s threat landscape to ensure alignment with the specific threats it faces.

Assessing Quality and Reliability

The quality and reliability of threat intelligence feeds are evaluated based on trustworthiness and variety of information sources, range and depth of coverage, and if they offer contextual analysis and dashboarding capabilities. To ensure threat intelligence feeds are truly actionable, organizations should routinely monitor data reliability and confirm that the feed’s data sources are relevant to their industry’s specific threats.

Selecting high-fidelity threat intelligence feeds requires assessing vendors for their credibility and the historical reliability of their feeds. This assessment can be measured against their success rate in correlating with previous incidents.

Balancing Cost and Value

While many threat intelligence feeds are free to use, commercial feeds typically require an annual subscription that can range from a few thousand dollars to over $100,000 per year. Organizations should align their choice of threat intelligence feeds with the budget they have available for cybersecurity efforts.

To ensure cost-effectiveness, organizations need to evaluate whether a threat intelligence feed provides unique value that justifies its cost and avoids redundancy with other feeds.

Top Threat Intelligence Feeds to Consider

When it comes to threat intelligence feeds, there are numerous options to consider.

  • The Internet Storm Center: is recognized for providing thorough explanations of threats.
  • Spamhaus: specializes in email security and anti-spam, offering robust solutions in that domain.
  • URLhaus: primarily addresses IP address and domain name anomalies and is best suited for network operators, ISPs, CERTs, and domain registries.
  • AlienVault OTX feeds: are accessible through detailed dashboards, which provide Pulses to summarize threats and display various indicators of compromise.
  • Recorded Future Threat Intelligence: while not a traditional feed, our intelligence cloud platform represents a significant advancement in threat intelligence. We automate the curation of intelligence feeds, streamlining the process to help you identify and prioritize threats more efficiently.

When they first appeared, threat intelligence feeds represented a huge leap forward, enabling security professionals to manage more relevant information than ever before. As the cyber threat intelligence cycle evolved, it became apparent that the abundance of free feeds in particular became “noisy” and filled with errors and false positives. These issues, coupled with the sheer volume of data available, started to pose problems.

Instead of viewing dozens of feeds separately, using a threat intelligence platform not only combines them all but also curates and compares the internal telemetry, generating customized alerts for your incident response and threat intelligence team.

The most powerful intelligence platforms, like the Recorded Future Intelligence Cloud, automatically curate intelligence feeds, sifting through data to identify and prioritize threat intelligence for your organization to action.

How to implement threat intelligence feeds in your organization

Implementing threat intelligence feeds in an organization is a critical step towards enhancing cybersecurity. It involves integrating with the existing infrastructure, training and awareness, and ongoing evaluation and optimization. Before the implementation, it’s essential to assess the organization’s cybersecurity infrastructure and gain executive support.

Ensure that the current cybersecurity solutions, such as SIEM or EDR systems, can integrate with the selected threat intelligence feeds to function properly. Develop and deliver comprehensive training programs to educate staff on the operational procedures and benefits of threat intelligence feeds. Lastly, establish protocols for regular review and optimization of threat intelligence feeds to maintain their relevance and effectiveness.

Identify key stakeholders within the organization and involve them in planning the adoption of threat intelligence feeds.

Integration with Existing Infrastructure

Integrating threat intelligence feeds with existing tools can extend these tools’ useful life and improve their return on investment. Organizations should combine third-party threat intelligence with their own local intelligence sources for a more comprehensive coverage.

Training and Awareness

Training security teams is critical to leveraging threat intelligence feeds, ensuring they understand how to employ this information effectively. Security personnel must be trained to differentiate and respond efficiently to high-priority alerts to take timely action against critical threats.

Proper training includes measures to manage alert volume and prevent SOC alert fatigue-related burnout by focusing on significant, actionable alerts.
